title: How are you handling discontinued voltage regulators and other EOL semiconductors in 2026?
gist: A forum poster describes end-of-life (EOL) pressure on legacy voltage regulators and PMICs worsening noticeably since 2024 for small-to-mid-volume (1k-50k units/year) industrial and embedded hardware makers, citing a TI TPS7A4501 going NRND after 2018-era production and open-market quotes running 2-6x original price, and asks the community how they source, verify and decide whether to redesign around EOL parts.

themes.theme: Worsening EOL pressure on legacy analog/power parts

insights.claim: The poster reports that EOL pressure on basic components has gotten noticeably worse since 2024 for small-to-mid volume (1,000-50,000 units/year) industrial and embedded hardware projects, hitting harder over the prior 12 months.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A grassroots practitioner report of accelerating EOL pressure since 2024 is an early, ground-level signal of legacy analog/power semiconductor supply tightening that could presage broader component shortages for industrial OEMs before it shows up in official distributor data.

insights.claim: Three recurring EOL categories are named: LDO/linear regulators from TI, Linear Tech (now part of ADI) and National Semiconductor that went not-recommended-for-new-designs (NRND) years ago but still ship in millions of legacy boards; PMICs paired with older SoCs that typically disappear within a quarter or two after the SoC vendor drops software support; and small-package discretes (SOT-23, SC-70) with long lead times even when not officially EOL.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A practical taxonomy of EOL-risk categories (legacy LDOs, SoC-tethered PMICs, small-package discretes) gives supply-chain and BOM-risk teams a checklist for proactively flagging at-risk parts before they hit NRND status.

insights.claim: The PMIC-obsolescence mechanism is causal: once a SoC vendor drops software support for an older SoC, the paired PMIC usually disappears within a quarter or two.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: This causal link (SoC software EOL triggers PMIC EOL within ~1-2 quarters) gives BOM managers a leading indicator — track SoC vendor support-lifecycle announcements as an early warning for paired power-IC discontinuation.

themes.theme: Cost and lead-time impact of a single NRND part

insights.claim: A TI TPS7A4501 linear regulator that a client has had in production since 2018 went NRND; the poster's team sourced it through a mix of authorized and open-market channels, with quotes ranging 2x to 6x the original price depending on lot size and traceability requirements, turning a routine order into a six-week scramble to keep a $200,000 purchase order moving.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A concrete 2-6x price premium and six-week delay on a single NRND part for a $200k PO quantifies the real cost-of-obsolescence tail risk in industrial BOMs, useful for benchmarking inventory-buffer or last-time-buy decisions.
insights.quote: Quotes are ranging 2x to 6x original price depending on lot size and traceability requirements — turned what should have been a routine order into a 6-week scramble to keep a $200k PO moving.

themes.theme: Open questions on sourcing strategy and counterfeit risk

insights.claim: The poster asks whether teams building regulated or mission-critical products (medical, industrial, automotive) are still redesigning around an EOL part or instead accepting the obsolescence price premium, noting the cost-versus-carrying trade-off has shifted noticeably for their team.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: This redesign-vs-pay-premium decision framework is directly relevant to component distributors and design-service firms positioning themselves around EOL mitigation, and signals rising willingness to pay premiums rather than requalify designs.

insights.claim: The poster says their team has been testing every incoming lot from independent distributors (decapsulation, electrical testing, sometimes X-ray) because the counterfeit problem in the open market has not gone away, and asks how smaller teams without that testing capability are managing trust in independent distributors.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Persistent counterfeit risk requiring decap/X-ray incoming inspection on open-market EOL parts is a tailwind for third-party component-authentication and counterfeit-detection service providers serving smaller OEMs that lack in-house testing.
